title: Ship an API: declare, generate a client, use it, change it, package it
summary: One declaration is the service, its OpenAPI document and the source of a typed client. An app uses it, the data it generates is analysed, an agent changes the contract, and the service is packaged as a reproducible image. Every step is a real run of a cancho tool; the seams that do not meet are shown as they are.
source: A recorded run of the real tools, replayed, on synthetic users (examples/ship-an-api/app.py): nothing here measures a real service. cancho-web's own users example is the service.

steps.note: Build the service from its one declaration (routes, bodies, errors), and start it. The compiler is the revision cancho-web pins.
steps.cmd: (cd cancho-web && scripts/build.sh examples/users/users.cho ../users-v1); ./users-v1 18950 2> serve.log &  curl -s localhost:18950/health

steps.note: A bad request is refused with every error at once, each with its JSON Pointer, as problem+json.
steps.cmd: curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"","age":151}' localhost:18950/users > refusal.json; for p in /count /errors/0 /errors/1; do jsonq -p $p --format text refusal.json; done

steps.note: The OpenAPI 3.1 document comes from the same declaration, so a route cannot be served and undocumented.
steps.cmd: curl -s localhost:18950/openapi.json > openapi.json; jsonq -p /paths --keys --format text openapi.json

steps.note: Frontend: a typed client from the server's own document. clientgen reads it, lists what it found, and writes Python.
steps.cmd: clientgen openapi.json --check; clientgen openapi.json --model | head -3; clientgen openapi.json --python -o client.py
steps.out:
ok 5 operations, 4 components
get /health -> health (0 parameters, body none, 1 responses: 200=object )
get /users -> listUsers (2 parameters, body none, 2 responses: 200=Page 422=Problem )
post /users -> createUser (0 parameters, body NewUser, 5 responses: 201=User 400=Problem 415=Problem 422=Problem 503=Problem )

steps.note: The client's annotations promise a dataclass. Does it return one? (A read-only call, so the service stays empty. An earlier build of clientgen returned a plain dict here; that is fixed in cancho-client-gen#15.)
steps.cmd: seek --format text 'def listUsers' client.py; python3 -c "import client; r = client.Client('http://127.0.0.1:18950').listUsers(limit=1); print(type(r).__name__, r)"
steps.out:
client.py:79:    def listUsers(self, *, limit: int | None = None, offset: int | None = None) -> Page:
Page Page(total=0, items=[])

steps.note: The app (a stand-in for whatever uses the service) registers 200 users through the client. Some are invalid on purpose.
What did the launch traffic get back, and which fields were refused?
steps.cmd: table --group status --agg count --sort status --format csv requests.csv; table --where "status = 422" --group field --agg count --sort -count --format csv requests.csv

steps.note: What does the service hold now? Ages of the registered users, and how many are over 120. (table compares text unless a column says :int.)
steps.cmd: stats describe users.csv --cols age > ages.json; for k in count mean max; do echo "$k $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/$k --format text ages.json)"; done; echo "older than 120: $(table --where 'age:int > 120' --agg count --format csv users.csv | tail -1)"

chart.title: Ages of the users the service holds (stats' exact histogram)

steps.note: An agent proposes a tighter limit: no age above 120. replace edits the one line of the declaration, and refuses unless it matches exactly once.
steps.cmd: replace --root cancho-web --old 'schema.new_int(heap, s2, 0, 150)' --new 'schema.new_int(heap, s2, 0, 120)' --expect 1 examples/users/users.cho | jsonq -p /data/replacements --format text -

steps.note: Rebuild it as a static executable (the linker wrapper adds -static) and restart. The served document now says 120.
steps.cmd: (cd cancho-web && CC=static-cc scripts/build.sh examples/users/users.cho ../users-v2); ./users-v2 18950 2> serve.log &  curl -s localhost:18950/openapi.json > openapi2.json; for f in openapi openapi2; do echo "$f: max age $(jsonq -p /components/schemas/NewUser/properties/age/maximum --format text $f.json)"; done
steps.out:
openapi: max age 150
openapi2: max age 120

steps.note: Does the client need regenerating? The limit lives in the server's schema.
steps.cmd: clientgen openapi2.json --python -o client2.py; diff client.py client2.py > /dev/null && echo 'client unchanged'

steps.note: A 130-year-old customer, who was valid yesterday.
steps.cmd: curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Old","age":130}' localhost:18950/users > old.json; jsonq -p /errors/0 --format text old.json

steps.note: Package it. A dynamically linked program is refused by rule; the static one becomes an image, built twice into two directories: the same binary gives the same image. (Two builds of the source differ by 2 bytes, so a fresh build has a new digest.)
steps.cmd: mkdir -p root img0/blobs/sha256 img/blobs/sha256 img2/blobs/sha256; cp users-v1 root/users; oci-build --root root --out img0 --platform linux/amd64 --bin users:app/users; cp users-v2 root/users; oci-build --root root --out img --platform linux/amd64 --bin users:app/users; oci-build --root root --out img2 --platform linux/amd64 --bin users:app/users; diff -r img img2 && echo 'the two images are identical'
steps.out:
refused: elf-dynamic (app/users)
sha256:b7a58f0d56b285d248bc8781fa69f0e66ea7096e4bb1e64e7a8610c03da290fa
sha256:b7a58f0d56b285d248bc8781fa69f0e66ea7096e4bb1e64e7a8610c03da290fa
the two images are identical

steps.note: What may the service do? The compiler proved it.
steps.cmd: (cd cancho-web && cancho authority examples/users/users.cho src/*.cho build/deps/*.cho --std | awk '/provably pure/{exit}{print}' | tr -s ' \n' ' ')
steps.out: performs args clock conn_accept conn_read conn_write err_write heap net_in("") poll never touches the filesystem signals other programs foreign code
